title: The shape of the loss decides how fast training goes: curvature, condition number and why optimizers behave differently
summary: Near a minimum a loss looks like a bowl whose curvatures are the eigenvalues of the Hessian. Gradient descent must keep its step below 2 over the largest curvature, so it crawls along the flattest direction; the ratio of largest to smallest curvature, the condition number, sets how many steps it needs. Momentum, preconditioning and rescaling the inputs all work by changing that ratio, and a slice through the landscape is the way to look at it.

media.alt: A semi-transparent three-dimensional surface with many peaks and valleys over a square of x1 and x2 from minus 3 to 3, with an amber search path of about 26 points from a rose square near the top right to a teal star in a valley near the middle.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F7.2 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard optimisation theory (quadratic model, gradient descent, heavy-ball momentum). The figure is the design system's synthetic F7.2 render of a many-valley test function, not a training loss of any project. Every number was computed for this page with NumPy by script, on a two-variable quadratic with curvatures 1 and 100.

read_the_figure.question: Where does a search on this surface travel, and what in the shape of the surface would slow it down or trap it?
read_the_figure.axes: x1 and x2: the two parameters, from -3 to 3, on the floor of the box. Vertical: the loss f(x), from 0 to about 55.
look_at: The start (square) and the end (star): is the direction of the search clear?
Whether the path goes steadily downhill or climbs a ridge on the way; a gradient method only goes downhill, a stochastic one may not.
How many valleys lie between start and end: each is a local minimum.
How steep the walls are compared with the floor of a valley: a long thin valley is the picture of a large condition number.
read_the_figure.proves: One path on one surface: that this search reached the lowest valley in this run. It cannot show that the same optimizer will do so on another start, or that the real training loss looks like this.
if_wrong: Reading a 3D surface from one viewing angle: the end marker can hide behind a peak.
Taking a low-dimensional slice for the whole landscape: a loss with a million parameters is only seen along a chosen line or plane.
Judging steepness from the colour scale instead of the vertical axis.
must_check: Path drawn on or above the surface.
For a slice of a real loss: which two directions were chosen and how they were scaled.

terms.meaning: The value of the loss as a function of the parameters: a surface over parameter space, whose minima are the trained models.
The vector of partial derivatives of the loss; it points uphill, so descent moves against it.
The matrix of second derivatives: the local curvature of the loss in every direction.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest Hessian eigenvalue at a minimum: how elongated the bowl is.
The step size of gradient descent. On a quadratic it must stay below 2 divided by the largest eigenvalue.
A running average of past steps that is added to the new one; it damps the zigzag across a valley and speeds the run along it.
Multiplying the gradient by a matrix, or rescaling the variables, so that the effective bowl is rounder.
A minimum with large or small Hessian eigenvalues: the same parameter error costs much more loss at a sharp one.

remember: Near a minimum, $L(\theta^{*}+\delta)\approx L(\theta^{*})+\tfrac12\,\delta^{\top}H\delta$: curvature is all that matters locally.
Gradient descent on a quadratic: each eigen-direction shrinks by the factor $1-\eta\lambda_i$ per step. It converges when $\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}$.
With the best fixed step $\eta=2/(\lambda_{\min}+\lambda_{\max})$ the error shrinks by $(\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)$ per step, so the number of steps grows in proportion to $\kappa$.
Heavy-ball momentum with tuned parameters shrinks the error by $(\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1)$ per step: the steps grow like $\sqrt\kappa$ instead of $\kappa$.
Standardising the inputs of a least-squares fit changes the Hessian $A^{\top}A/m$ and can bring $\kappa$ close to 1.
Newton's method uses $H^{-1}\nabla L$ and is unaffected by $\kappa$ on a quadratic, at the price of forming and solving with $H$.

understand.title: Easy: a valley with a gentle slope
understand.text: A ball in a long, narrow valley rolls quickly down the steep walls and then crawls along the floor. A walker who takes steps of a fixed size must keep them small enough not to jump across the valley, and so takes forever along the floor. The tighter the valley, the worse it is. The Hessian eigenvalues are the steepness of the walls and of the floor.

understand.title: Medium: one number for the whole story
understand.text: On the bowl $\tfrac12(\lambda_1x^2+\lambda_2y^2)$ the step must obey $\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}$ or the steep direction diverges, and then the flat direction moves by only the fraction $\eta\lambda_{\min}$ of its distance per step. The ratio $\kappa$ is therefore the number of steps, up to a constant. Rescaling a variable changes $\lambda$ for that direction, which is why unscaled inputs of very different size give an ill-conditioned loss.

understand.title: Hard: what each optimizer changes
understand.text: Momentum changes the dynamics from a first-order to a second-order recursion whose best contraction depends on $\sqrt\kappa$. Adaptive methods such as Adam divide each coordinate by a running estimate of its gradient size, which acts as a diagonal preconditioner; it helps when the bad scaling is along the coordinate axes and not when the valley is tilted. Second-order methods change the metric itself. L-BFGS builds an approximate inverse Hessian from past gradients.

understand.title: Hardest: a real loss is not a quadratic
understand.text: Away from a minimum the Hessian changes from point to point, may have negative eigenvalues (saddles), and for a network has a few large eigenvalues and very many near zero. Sharpness measures are not invariant to reparametrisation: rescaling two layers in opposite ways leaves the function unchanged but changes the Hessian eigenvalues. So claims such as flat minima generalise better need care, and a slice plot is evidence about one direction only.

steps.title: A loss near its minimum is a quadratic
steps.note: The gradient vanishes at the minimum, so the quadratic term leads. Rotating into the eigenvectors $Q$ of $H$ separates the problem into independent one-dimensional bowls with curvatures $\lambda_i$. Atlas S13 example 4, the least-squares error surface of a line fit, is exactly such a bowl.

steps.title: Gradient descent contracts each direction
steps.note: A direction converges when $|1-\eta\lambda_i|<1$, which for every direction at once means $0<\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}$. The same condition appears as the stability limit of explicit Euler on a stiff decay: gradient descent is explicit Euler on the gradient flow $\dot\theta=-\nabla L$. See the stiffness concept page.

steps.title: The best step and the rate
steps.note: Balancing the fastest and the slowest directions gives this contraction. Checked numerically for curvatures 1 and 100 ($\kappa=100$): $\rho=0.9802$, and the loss, which falls by $\rho^2$ per step, dropped by a factor of $10^6$ in 346 steps against a predicted 345.4.

steps.title: Momentum improves the rate to the square root
steps.note: On the same problem the heavy-ball method needed 58 steps for the same $10^6$ drop instead of 346, with $\beta=0.669$ and $\eta=0.0331$ (computed). Its per-step contraction is $(\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1)=0.818$. The tuning needs the two extreme eigenvalues, which are unknown in practice, so real runs use a fixed $\beta$ such as 0.9 and a schedule.

steps.title: Rescaling changes the conditioning
steps.tex: H=\frac1m A^{\top}A,\qquad A\to A\,D^{-1}\ (D=\text{column standard deviations})
steps.note: For a two-column design matrix with one column ten times larger, the Hessian had eigenvalues 0.966 and 101.45, $\kappa=105$; after dividing each column by its standard deviation the eigenvalues were 0.954 and 1.057, $\kappa=1.11$ (computed, seed 0). This is why the playground normalises its channels before training, and why the power-mean and scaled losses of the Playground pages change the speed and not only the numbers.

steps.title: A slice is a one-dimensional picture of curvature
steps.note: Pick a direction $d$ (a gradient, an eigenvector, a random vector scaled to the weights) and plot the loss along it. The second derivative of the slice is $d^{\top}Hd$, the curvature in that direction. Two slices through the same minimum can look completely different, so name the direction and its length scale.

steps.title: Sharp against flat
steps.tex: \Delta L\approx\tfrac12\lambda\,\varepsilon^2\quad\text{for a parameter error }\varepsilon\text{ along an eigen-direction}
steps.note: With curvatures 1 and 100 and an error of 0.1, the loss rises by 0.005 along the flat direction and 0.5 along the sharp one: a hundredfold (computed). A model that must be rounded, perturbed or retrained on slightly different data is safer sitting in the flat part.

steps.title: Newton and preconditioning remove the ratio
steps.note: On a quadratic one Newton step reaches the minimum whatever $\kappa$ is. Using the diagonal of the Hessian as a preconditioner gave $\kappa=1$ on the test bowl because it was already diagonal; for a tilted bowl a diagonal scaling cannot do it, which is the limit of the adaptive methods.

worked.title: How many gradient steps does a bowl with curvatures 1 and 100 need, with and without momentum?
worked.problem: The loss is $L(x,y)=\tfrac12(x^2+100y^2)$, started at $(1,1)$. Find the largest stable step, the best fixed step, the per-step contraction and the number of steps for the loss to fall by $10^{-6}$, then compare with heavy-ball momentum.

solution.text: The loss falls by $\rho^2$ per step, so the steps needed are
Heavy ball with $\eta=0.0331$, $\beta=0.669$: contraction per step.

worked.answer: Gradient descent: stable only below $\eta=0.02$, best step 0.0198, contraction 0.980 per step, about 345 steps (the run took 346). Heavy ball: contraction 0.818 per step, 58 steps in the run. Momentum bought a factor of six, close to the ratio $\kappa/\sqrt\kappa=10$ allowing for constants. Standardising the variables would have made $\kappa=1$ and one step enough.

analyze.q: A training curve falls fast for 50 steps and then almost flat for thousands, while the loss is still high. Give two explanations that this page supports and say how each would be tested.
analyze.hint: A long flat valley (large kappa), or a saddle or plateau. Look at the Hessian eigenvalues, or at the gradient norm.

analyze.q: Two slices through the same trained network, along two random directions of the same length, look very different: one is a narrow V, the other almost flat. What does it say about the Hessian?
analyze.hint: The curvature of a slice is d^T H d.

analyze.q: Why does doubling the learning rate sometimes make the loss explode after hundreds of calm steps?
analyze.hint: The largest curvature can grow during training; compare eta with 2 over it.

evaluate.q: A paper reports that its optimizer converges faster than Adam on a quadratic with kappa = 10. What would you ask before accepting that this carries over to a neural network?
evaluate.hint: Tuned learning rates for both, several seeds, the Hessian spectrum of the real loss, and equal budgets.

evaluate.q: Is a flat minimum always better? Consider the rescaling of two successive layers by c and 1/c.
evaluate.hint: The function is unchanged but the Hessian eigenvalues change.

create: Design a small experiment that measures the largest Hessian eigenvalue of a loss during training without forming the Hessian (use Hessian-vector products and power iteration) and plots it against the learning rate used.
Draw a landscape slice for a least-squares problem with two inputs of very different scale, before and after standardising, with contours at the same loss levels.
Propose a fair way to compare two optimizers on a landscape with many valleys, using equal evaluation budgets and several starts.

checks.q: Why must the gradient-descent step stay below 2 over the largest eigenvalue?
checks.hint: Look at the factor 1 - eta*lambda for the steepest direction.
checks.answer: The error in that direction is multiplied by $1-\eta\lambda_{\max}$ each step. When $\eta\lambda_{\max}>2$ that factor is below $-1$, so its size exceeds one and the error grows with alternating sign: the steep direction diverges however flat the others are.

checks.q: A bowl has curvatures 4 and 400. What is kappa, the largest stable step, and the best fixed step?
checks.answer: $\kappa=100$, $\eta<2/400=0.005$, best fixed step $2/404=0.00495$ (calculated). The contraction is $99/101=0.980$ per step.

checks.q: Why does standardising the inputs help a least-squares fit trained with gradient descent?
checks.hint: What is the Hessian of the squared error?
checks.answer: The Hessian is $A^{\top}A/m$, so the curvature in a coordinate grows with the square of the scale of its input column. A column ten times larger has a hundred times the curvature. Dividing each column by its standard deviation puts the diagonal near 1 and the eigenvalue spread near 1: in the check kappa fell from 105 to 1.11.

checks.q: A claim says that this minimum is flat, so the model is robust. What is missing?
checks.answer: Which directions were measured (the sharpest, or random ones), at what length, and in what parametrisation. A flat reading along random directions can coexist with a sharp one along a few. Sharpness changes if the layers are rescaled in opposite ways although the function is identical, so the claim needs a reparametrisation-aware measure or a direct test such as the loss after rounding or perturbing the weights.

checks.q: You can afford only 20 Hessian-vector products. How do you estimate the largest curvature of the loss at a trained point?
checks.answer: Start from a random unit vector $u$, repeat $u\leftarrow Hu/\|Hu\|$ with each product obtained by differentiating the gradient along $u$ (the Hessian is never formed). The Rayleigh quotient $u^{\top}Hu$ converges to $\lambda_{\max}$; twenty iterations give a usable estimate when the top eigenvalue is well separated. Compare $2/\hat\lambda_{\max}$ with the learning rate in use.
